segments.text: Part 2. You will hear a manager talking to a group of new staff on the day before a summer music festival opens. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Briefing for festival staff

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Larkmoor Music Festival. My name's Claire Hollis, and I'm the staff manager, so for the next four days I'm the person you'll see running around with a clipboard. Before we hand out uniforms, I want to go through a few things: the jobs, your shifts, the rules, and who to contact when something goes wrong. It shouldn't take more than a quarter of an hour.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Right, jobs first. Most of you applied for a particular role, and we've tried to give everyone what they asked for. Bar work, for example, is completely full now, and so is ticket scanning at the entrance gates, so we won't be moving anyone into those teams.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Where we're really short is in the car parks, directing the traffic, and in the recycling team, picking up litter. Most visitors arrive on Thursday afternoon, sorry, Friday afternoon, so that's when the car parks are busiest. Litter picking isn't glamorous, I know, but it's often the job people enjoy most by Sunday. The information tents, on the other hand, have more than enough volunteers already.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Okay, shifts. Each one is six hours, not eight, as it said in some of the old adverts. You need to sign in at the crew check-in tent at least fifteen minutes before you start. Every shift includes a thirty-minute break, and before anyone asks, yes, you're paid for it.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: A few of you have asked about night shifts. There's no extra pay for those, I'm afraid, but you do get the following day off. And the rota is drawn up by my team, so you can't pick your own shifts online, although you can ask to change them, which I'll come back to.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Now, rules. Some of them might surprise you. Phones, for instance: we'd actually like you to keep them switched on, because we send updates to a staff group chat. And photos are fine anywhere, even backstage, as long as you don't post the backstage ones online.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: But there are two rules we're very strict about. You mustn't drink alcohol while you're wearing your staff T-shirt, even after your shift if you haven't changed. And your wristband is for you alone, so no bringing friends or family onto the site, not even for half an hour. Oh, and footwear: trainers are fine, you don't need safety boots, just nothing open-toed.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Right, the last thing, and probably the most important, is who to contact. You'll get a card with all the numbers on, but let me go through it. If you need to change a shift, say you've swapped with a friend, you might think your area supervisor can sort it out, but they can't. That has to go through the staff office, which is the green cabin behind the main stage.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.say: If your wristband gets damaged, or you lose it, go to the accreditation desk at the staff entrance. They'll print you a new one, but it costs fifteen pounds, so do look after it.
turns.text: If your wristband gets damaged, or you lose it, go to the accreditation desk at the staff entrance. They'll print you a new one, but it costs £15, so do look after it.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Next, unattended bags. Please don't pick them up and carry them over to lost property, and don't open them. Just radio security control and stay nearby until someone arrives.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Something that happens every year is a child who's lost their parents. Your first thought might be to call security, or to take them to the medical centre, but neither is right unless the child's hurt. Walk them to the information point by the main gate, because that's where our welfare team is based.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.say: If there's a problem with your meal vouchers, so you haven't been given any, or a food stall won't accept them, speak to the catering manager. Each voucher's worth eight pounds, by the way, and you get two per shift. And if you're running late, don't ring the staff office, because they won't pass the message on in time. Call your area supervisor directly, since they're the one who'll need to find cover.
turns.text: If there's a problem with your meal vouchers, so you haven't been given any, or a food stall won't accept them, speak to the catering manager. Each voucher's worth £8, by the way, and you get two per shift. And if you're running late, don't ring the staff office, because they won't pass the message on in time. Call your area supervisor directly, since they're the one who'll need to find cover.
turns.speaker: manager

turns.text: Finally, if you hurt yourself while you're working, even if it's only a small cut, you must go to the medical centre so it's recorded. Don't just ask a colleague for a plaster. Oh, and if you miss the last staff shuttle bus back to town, the transport desk closes at midnight, so plan ahead. Right, any questions before we hand out the T-shirts?
turns.speaker: manager

turns.heard: Good morning everyone and welcome to the Larkmoor Music Festival. My name's Claire Hollis and I'm the staff manager, so for the next four days I'm the person you'll see running around with a clipboard. Before we hand out uniforms, I want to go through a few things. The jobs, your shifts, the rules, and who to contact when something goes wrong. It shouldn't take more than a quarter of an hour.

Right, jobs first. Most of you applied for a particular role and we've tried to give everyone what they asked for. Bar work, for example, is completely full now and so is ticket scanning at the entrance gates so we won't be moving anyone into those teams.

Where we're really short is in the car parks, directing the traffic, and in the recycling team, picking up litter. Most visitors arrive on Friday afternoon, so that's when the car parks are busiest. Litter picking isn't glamorous, I know, but it's often the job people enjoy most by Sunday. The information tents, on the other hand, have more than enough volunteers already.

Okay, shifts. Each one is six hours, not eight as it said in some of the old adverts. You need to sign in at the crew check-in tent at least 15 minutes before you start. Every shift includes a 30 minute break, and before anyone asks, yes, you're paid for it.

A few of you have asked about night shifts. There's no extra pay for those, I'm afraid, but you do get the following day off. And the rota is drawn up by my team, so you can't pick your own shifts online, although you can ask to change them, which I'll come back to.

Now, rules. Some of them might surprise you. Phones, for instance, we'd actually like you to keep them switched on because we send updates to a staff group chat. And photos are fine anywhere, even backstage, as long as you don't post the backstage ones online.

But there are two rules we're very strict about. You mustn't drink alcohol while you're wearing your staff T-shirt, even after your shift if you haven't changed. And your wristband is for you alone, so no bringing friends or family onto the site, not even for half an hour. Oh, and footwear. Trainers are fine – you don't need safety boots, just nothing open-toed.

Right, the last thing, and probably the most important, is who to contact. You'll get a card with all the numbers on, but let me go through it. If you need to change a shift – say you've swapped with a friend – you might think your area supervisor can sort it out, but they can't. That has to go through the staff office, which is the green cabin behind the main stage.
If your wristband gets damaged or you lose it, go to the accreditation desk at the staff entrance. They'll print you a new one, but it costs £15, so do look after it.
Next, unattended bags: please don't pick them up and carry them over to lost property, and don't open them. Just radio security control and stay nearby until someone arrives.

Something that happens every year is a child who's lost their parents. Your first thought might be to call security, or to take them to the medical centre, but neither is right unless the child's hurt. Walk them to the information point by the main gate, because that's where our welfare team is based.

If there's a problem with your meal vouchers – so you haven't been given any, or a food stall won't accept them – speak to the catering manager. Each voucher's worth eight pounds, by the way, and you get two per shift. And if you're running late, don't ring the staff office because they won't pass the message on in time. Call your area supervisor directly, since they're the one who'll need to find cover.

Finally, if you hurt yourself while you're working, even if it's only a small cut, you must go to the medical centre so it's recorded. Don't just ask a colleague for a plaster.
